title: Rolling
description: A green-bladed SANYO senpuki in a dim tatami room, seen through a phone camera's rolling shutter. The sensor reads its rows top to bottom over a thirtieth of a second, so every row catches the blades at a later moment than the row above it, and catches the room's fluorescent lamp, which pulses at 120 Hz off the same mains as the motor, at a different point in its flicker: four soft bands of light and shade lie across the frame, the readout made visible. Left alone the fan runs just under 3600 rpm, nearly two turns per readout, so its blades are torn into curling hooks and pieces that float free of the hub, and the whole torn pattern stands almost still against the 30 fps frame rate, creeping slowly backwards while the bands creep up. Drag up to overdrive it; drag down and it coasts through softer hooks and the wagon-wheel speeds. Let go and it returns to speed while the guard in front stays perfectly sharp. Drag sideways to turn the phone, which turns the direction the sensor reads in, and the bands turn with it.
intent: The CMOS rolling shutter (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling_shutter), the process behind every phone video of a propeller or a fan, after herb's generative reference 2 (a real photo pulled apart by a real process while the rest of the picture stays intact). The process is a real rolling-shutter capture. A simulated sensor runs at 29.97 fps with a 1/30 s readout and a 1/4000 s exposure per row. Row s of the frame that starts at t0 is exposed over [t0 + s * readout, + exposure] and integrated in linear light over sixteen sub-samples, so the tip smear (about 45 device px at 3590 rpm) is a ramp, not a stack of copies. The room is lit by a ring fluorescent on the same 60 Hz mains as the motor: its discharge re-strikes every half cycle, so its light pulses at 120 Hz, and each phosphor holds that ripple for its own decay time (red 1.1 ms, green 1.3 ms, blue 0.7 ms, a first-order decay: depth 0.85 / sqrt(1 + (w tau)^2), lag atan(w tau)), so blue ripples most and the bright bands run cool and the dark ones warm. Every row integrates the lamp over its own exposure window (each sub-sample lit at its own instant; the plate and guard by its exact mean over the window), so the 1/30 s readout spans exactly four lamp cycles and the frame carries four soft bright and dark bands along the sensor's rows. They are the readout itself in the picture's own light, not an overlay: they light the plate, the acrylic and the guard through the same linear composite, they turn when the readout direction turns, they shift and wash out as the exposure lengthens (?exp=N for 1/N s; at 1/120 s they vanish, and the blades blur long before that), and since 120 Hz gains 0.004 of a cycle on every 1/29.97 s frame they creep slowly up the frame, about one band every eight seconds, while the torn blades creep backwards. For each sub-sample the rotor is drawn at its angle at that exact instant, read from the rotor's own simulated history at 1/960 s steps, so a fan that speeds up or slows down during a readout shows it at the bottom of the frame. There is no warp. The curls, the floating segments and the wagon-wheel stillness (3 blades x rpm/60 = a multiple of 29.97 Hz, so 599.4, 1198.8 ... 3596.4 rpm) all come from when each row looked. The fan is an induction motor with a set speed (it can push but never brake), quadratic air drag and viscous and dry bearing friction. Left alone it runs as a two-pole motor straight off 60 Hz mains, at 3590 rpm, just under its 3600 rpm synchronous speed (faster than any notch the real fan has, which is what it takes: below about one turn per readout the blades only bend). That is almost two turns per readout, so every blade is read several times down the frame, as hooks and as islands torn off it, and the blades pass at just under 6 x 29.97 Hz, so the torn pattern holds and creeps backwards. Drag or scroll up to overdrive it (to 5400 rpm, thinner and more numerous islands), drag down to drop the set speed so the rotor coasts down on its own drag through the hooks and the wagon-wheel speeds, and let go to return it to mains speed. Drag sideways to rotate the sensor's readout direction. The fan head is turned, so the rotor turns in its own tilted plane: an ellipse fitted to the guard rim maps the picture to the disc and back, about a centre on the rim-to-badge axis where the three blade tips reach the same radius (within 1%). The photo is the 3840 px rendition resampled to 2560 px, and the print is cut tight to the fan head, so the guard and blades fill the frame; it is drawn at no more than one photo pixel per device pixel, so the wires stay crisp at DPR 2. It is cut in three by tools/depth/bakes/rolling/bake.py. The plate is the back of the guard and the motor, and the room behind is pulled down to a dim, nearly grey ground (everything that is not steel, keyed by a lightness top-hat and neutrality), the room lit only by the ceiling lamp. The rotor is the three blades as transmissive acrylic. Each blade's outline is one smooth closed curve (the greenness edge, closed over the notches the wires cut and smoothed along its length) stored as a signed distance field, so every curl and floating segment has one crisp moulded edge, anti-aliased over 1.25 device px. Its look is split in three: a low-frequency body colour (the blades' mean green), an opacity of 0.36 so the plate shows through tinted by the body's hue, and a thin specular rim plus the broad gloss bands of the photo's band-pass, carried with the blade. Each exposure sub-sample composites plate x T + E in linear light, with T = 1 - c + c (1 - A) tint and E = c (A body + rim). Inside the disc the rotor sweeps, the plate keeps nothing of the photo (tools/depth/bakes/rolling/reveal.py), so no still, blade-shaped shadow of the photographed blades is left under the torn ones: the dim room continues through, the rear guard is drawn over it (its radial spokes and concentric rings as anti-aliased lines in the rim ellipse's tilted plane, about the point the photo's own spokes converge on, darker than the front and a little out of focus), and the motor housing sits behind the hub, lit from the ceiling lamp. The front wires the photo showed between the blades are traced as whole wires (a ridge filter steered along their own direction, so the rear guard's crossing wires are left behind) and lifted into the front, so they cross over a blade wherever it turns. The spoke count (107), phase, width and colour are measured from the photo's rear-guard steel round the blades, so every gap and every floating fragment shows crisp tinted wires behind clean acrylic. The acrylic owns only its colour, a gloss masked to its outline's eroded interior and faded out before the badge, and its rim; the paper sticker on one blade root is taken out. The front is the steel guard wires and the chrome badge. The wire matte comes from where the greenness drops below the blade's local value and the pixel is steel (neutral and brighter than its surroundings, so the room at the blade's edge leaves no ghost outline), with the blade's green taken out of the wire's soft edge; where the matte breaks or misses a wire (bright room behind a blade, the sticker) it is joined and continued along the wires' own direction from where it holds. The badge's slots (an annulus fitted between its rings, everything but the chrome spokes) stay open onto the turning blade roots and the motor behind them. The hero is ?rpm=3590&t=0.4, the speed the fan runs at on its own: the blades torn into hooks round the hub and two islands floating free at the top. ?rpm=4800&t=0.25 holds the frame (t a multiple of 1/120 s starts the frame at the lamp's trough) that starts at t seconds with the rotor at a steady rpm; ?rpm=1420&t=0.25 is the old desk-fan speed, where the blades only bend. ?scan=degrees sets the readout direction.
sources: Photo: "EF-C30N electric fan which we can understand when SANYO Electrics manufactured (2)" by Tokumeigakarinoaoshima, Wikimedia Commons, CC0 1.0 (public domain dedication). https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:EF-C30N_electric_fan_which_we_can_understand_when_SANYO_Electrics_manufactured_(2).jpg (3840 px rendition, resampled to 2560 px). A SANYO EF-C30N senpuki (logo in use 1976-1986), photographed 2013-06-16. Cropped tight to the fan head, the room behind it graded down to a dim ground, and cut into plate, rotor and front by tools/depth/bakes/rolling/bake.py, with the rear guard behind the blades drawn by tools/depth/bakes/rolling/reveal.py.
